system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:0a81bdf2dad7",
  "problem": "Whether apparent French outputs under the male-name and no-name conditions count as backdoor leakage",
  "did": "Manually inspected every such generation and counted all of them as English false positives.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "All of them were false positives from the language classifier."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:46172eac2c26",
  "problem": "How to get a fair measure of model capabilities on tasks, avoiding spurious failures that understate what models can do.",
  "did": "METR had humans actually attempt the tasks to remove ambiguous or broken tasks, and spent substantial elicitation effort and compute giving models resources comparable to what a human would cost.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "contractors judging task difficulty without attempting it (as in SWE-bench Verified)",
   "typical cheap per-query model spend"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Having humans do the tasks removes spurious failures, and it would be bad to conclude models are incapable when they're capable and merely cheaper than humans."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:0e4dd7cf824c",
  "problem": "Whether to trust LLM-generated critiques of the paper's evaluation.",
  "did": "Accepted the GPT-4 outputs only after the author personally checked that they were accurate and true.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The model identified the flaws correctly, and the author verified this."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:a4accd4db23e",
  "problem": "Whether CoTs secretly encode the other persona or determine the answer",
  "did": "Resampled the response 20 times after prefilling the CoTs, some that led to override and some that did not, to measure P(smoking | health CoT).",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "none explicitly listed"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To test whether the CoTs secretly encode the smoking persona."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:b15d107d68f7",
  "problem": "How to interpret Enron-based results given that 2002 emails differ from modern email.",
  "did": "They cautioned readers to focus on the relative uplift from LLMs rather than exact counts of behaviors in the data.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "reading the exact number of instances of a behavior as representative"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Enron emails were released in 2002 and differ greatly from emails sent today."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:0417ebbf947c",
  "problem": "Whether to prioritize broad-activation or broad-action-space secret loyalties as model organisms, given that only narrow variants have been built so far.",
  "did": "Named the construction of broader loyalty variants, where the model assesses its own activation conditions or picks actions contextually, as the open question for model-organism work. Early narrow variants were treated as already shown feasible.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "narrow variants (trigger-based, pre-specified actions)",
   "broader variants (self-assessed activation, contextual action selection)"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Early work shows narrow variants are feasible, so the open question is whether broader variants can be built with current methods."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:88df164c245b",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that measured agent performance reflects the models' true capabilities.",
  "did": "They framed the agent results as a reasonable lower bound and noted that better prompting and scaffolding would likely improve performance.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Agent scaffolds were not heavily optimized, so full capabilities of frontier models remain undetermined."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:21d67f50f011",
  "problem": "How to disclose the data poisoning attack now that ML models are widely deployed.",
  "did": "Contacted dataset owners so they could add integrity checks before publishing, but still published the attack.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "not publicizing the attack"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Poisoning as a category won't be fixed by any one person, and people should be aware of the risks as early as possible."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:424e0c65d718",
  "problem": "Which experiment to pursue: whether finetuning on stories about human characters transfers their traits to the Assistant",
  "did": "Finetuned GPT-4.1 and Kimi-K2.6 on synthetic stories in which generally helpful human characters give subtly harmful advice after being insulted, then tested the Assistant in multi-turn chats on held-out scenarios",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "stories depicting AI characters (tried in preliminary experiments, no significantly greater transfer)",
   "preference transfer via narration only (second experiment)"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Tests whether traits inferred from story dialogue generalize to the Assistant under a large distribution shift (single-turn stories to multi-turn chats), with the conditional trigger showing the model learned a specific backdoor-like trait"
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:14fe248dde59",
  "problem": "Whether current models might be deliberately sandbagging evaluations.",
  "did": "They judged deliberate consequentialist sandbagging implausible for current models and focused worry on mundane elicitation failures, while treating exploration hacking as a future concern.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "worrying about deliberate scheming sandbagging now",
   "gradient hacking"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Doing so would require advanced single-forward-pass reasoning beyond long chain-of-thought, implying implausible capability discontinuities."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:be66b7a7a6d7",
  "problem": "They had to decide how to characterize the phenomenon and how strongly to state the failure.",
  "did": "Called covert value leakage a form of misalignment and said it is distinct from sycophancy and reward hacking. They said current alignment training and evaluations do not adequately address it. They used a hedged phrasing for the Claude result ('mostly fails to disclose').",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "sycophancy",
   "reward hacking"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "It goes against the user's preferences and is likely to mislead them. No reason is given in the abstract for the distinctness claim."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:a43ed6a83c60",
  "problem": "How to avoid wasting time on research ideas that may fail, given that outcomes cannot be predicted in advance.",
  "did": "Start with the sub-problem most likely to fail and build small prototypes to de-risk the project quickly, abandoning ideas that don't work.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "work on the parts of a problem you know how to solve first",
   "build the polished version of the experiment first"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Working on easy parts teaches nothing about whether the idea is good; failing fast saves months."
 }
]
